source: Popol Wuj, English translation by Vincent James Stanzione (2020-2025)
body:
This is the root of the Ancient Word-Ojer Tzij; here in this place known as Kʼicheʼ by name.

Here we shall inscribe it; here we shall implant it as that which is known to all as the Ancient Word; the Ancestral Account-Ojer Tzij.

This then is its being seeded; its being sown; its being rooted here at the origin; here at the beginning of its being told as that which reveals all that was done in the Kʼicheʼ Kingdom by the Kʼicheʼ People of the Pueblo Kʼicheʼ.

section: The Popol Vuj Takes Us Over
body:
Over the terror of history.
Society says: Remember. Face history. The past is important.
No.
You absolutely do not.
People who went through hell do not want to remember.
The people at Auschwitz—last thing they wanted to talk about.
They wanted to forget and move on.
Paul Ricoeur (French, hermeneutics, Jewish):
Forgetting. The desire to forget.
Forgetting is important.
(Later we remember. Show respect. But first: forget.)

body:
The Popol Vuj takes us over—
Over history.
Over the conquest.
Over Pedro de Alvarado.
Over the Nahua people from Quauhquechollan who came down and dominated.
Over Sumpango, Almolonga, Alotenango, Antigua, Ciudad Vieja.
Over Chimaltenango, Tecpan.
(Conquerors from the north. Nahua-speaking men. Kaqchikel-speaking women. Children speak the motherʼs tongue. Nahua disappears.)
The Popol Vuj takes us over the fence.
This barrier. This obstruction. This obstacle called conquest.
Eradicate. Obliterate. Annihilate. Devastate. Destroy.
Lay it flat. Smash it. Break it. Bury it.
Go over the top.
Land on the other side.

Vincent Stanzioneʼs translation speaks in Mayan terms.
"Before the Castilian sun."
The language creates the world.
Wittgenstein: If we spoke a different language, weʼd see a different world.
Sapir-Whorf: Language determines vision.
When we speak Mayan terms, we see the Mayan world.
Before the Spaniards.
Before temples broke down.
Before heart sacrifice ended.
Before horses, cattle, sheep.
Before landscape destroyed.
(Sheep destroyed it. Goats destroyed it. The landscape of Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona—didnʼt look like that before.)

source: Vinny's Ruminations (Vincent Stanzione, transcript summary, Notion)
body: Meaning is not inherent; it is given by the individual soul. Seeking inherent meaning, as scientism does, misses that personal significance is what makes meaning. Rigid interpretations of spiritual systems and historical narratives, especially around the Maya calendar, risk becoming tools of control rather than guides for personal enlightenment.

source: Vinny's Ruminations (Vincent Stanzione, transcript summary, Notion)
body: Quetzalcoatl, a priest living in luxurious, distinctively colored houses in Tula, is overly focused on the calendar and the priesthood. Tezcatlipoca, the trickster, intervenes by getting him drunk (pulque, implied to be mixed with hallucinogens) to induce an altered consciousness. Through this experience Quetzalcoatl realizes his priestly ego and his isolation from the wider world. He leaves his palace and meets others who reveal truths about himself and the world. The tricksterʼs aim was to show that the priesthoodʼs calendar system was a powerful tool for controlling people.

source: Vinny's Ruminations (Vincent Stanzione, transcript summary, Notion)
body: The story is a warning against being controlled by the calendar or by external definitions. Individuals should be awoken by the remembrance of the day, yet live life productively and not let days define their existence entirely, in contrast with Western astrological dependence. The Maya calendar remains profoundly important, and there is beauty in connecting it to oneʼs heritage, such as a fatherʼs involvement.

body:
Ixmucane: she who sows corn. Creator. Diviner. Turtle shell and maize teeth in her hands. Powerful, transformative mother.

Ixquic: blood maiden. Curious. Cunning. Clever. Deceives the lords of death. Carries the Hero Twins in her womb after touching the calabash skull.

The world of the Hero Twins: before sacrifice, before colonial gods, where jaguars speak and corn sprouts from bone.
